Write an off-host backup copy script and its tests for the fedbench database host.

CREATE EXACTLY THESE 2 FILES with the write tool now; do not summarise or ask:
  1. deploy/backup-offhost.sh
  2. tests/offhostBackup.test.ts

CONTEXT. /usr/local/bin/backup-fedbench.sh writes a nightly pair into /srv/fedbench/backups:
`fedbench-YYYY-MM-DD.dump` (pg_dump custom format) and `fedbench-YYYY-MM-DD.sql.gz`. Both live on
the SAME DISK as the database. There is currently no off-host copy at all, and an off-host copy is
a hard gate on migrating production data onto this box. Tomorrow the destination will be an
already-mounted NFS share at /mnt/nasbackup, but this script MUST NOT hardcode that.

WHAT backup-offhost.sh MUST DO:
  - Accept `--dest PATH` (required for a real run), `--source PATH` (default
    /srv/fedbench/backups), `--keep N` (default 14), `--check`, `--help`.
  - Select the newest *.dump by MTIME, not by filename sort: a job that wrote yesterday's NAME
    today is still a stale recovery point. Copy that file and its same-day .sql.gz twin.
  - VERIFY WHAT LANDED. This is the whole point of the script and the reason it is not `cp`.
    Compute sha256 of the source, copy, then compute sha256 of the file AT THE DESTINATION and
    require them to match. A truncated or short NFS write is the failure that matters here and it
    does not set a non-zero exit status. Also compare byte sizes and report both numbers on
    mismatch. If verification fails, REMOVE the partial destination file so a later run cannot
    mistake it for a good copy, and fail.
  - Write to a temporary name in the destination directory and rename into place only after
    verification passes, so an interrupted run never leaves a file with a final name. The rename
    must be within the same directory so it is atomic.
  - Never delete anything from the SOURCE. This script only ever adds to the destination.
  - Retention on the destination: keep the newest N pairs, remove older ones, and report how many
    were removed. Never remove the pair it just wrote. Refuse to prune if the current copy failed.
  - `--check` must probe writability of the destination by creating and removing a temp file
    there, must confirm the destination is not the same filesystem as the source (compare `stat
    -c %d` device numbers) and WARN loudly if it is -- a "off-host" copy on the same disk is the
    exact false assurance this script exists to prevent -- and must confirm the destination is a
    mountpoint (`mountpoint -q` if available) or warn that it may be a plain directory, because
    copying into the mountpoint of an unmounted NFS share silently fills the local root disk.
  - Print a summary line: what was copied, both sha256 values matching, total bytes, duration,
    and how many old pairs were pruned.

WHAT tests/offhostBackup.test.ts MUST DO. Run the script with spawnSync against temp directories
with fixture files. At minimum:
  - a healthy copy verifies and lands under the final name;
  - a CONTROL: corrupt the copy so the destination hash differs (shim `sha256sum` via PATH, or
    make the destination unwritable, whichever you can do reliably) and require a non-zero exit
    AND require that no file with the final name is left behind;
  - `--check` against an unwritable destination fails and changes nothing;
  - same-device source and destination produces the warning;
  - retention keeps N and removes older, and never removes the newest.


HOUSE STYLE -- read these existing files in the repo first and match them exactly:
  deploy/backup-fedbench.sh, deploy/fedbench-deadman.sh, deploy/alerting-install.sh,
  deploy/fedbench-backup.service, deploy/fedbench-backup.timer, deploy/fedbench-deadman.timer

Every shell script in deploy/ follows this shape:
  - `#!/usr/bin/env bash` then `set -uo pipefail`
  - A header comment block: what it does, 2-4 example invocations, and an "Undo:" line saying
    exactly what it changed and how to reverse it.
  - Helpers, verbatim:
      ok()   { printf '  \033[32mok\033[0m    %s\n' "$*"; }
      bad()  { printf '  \033[31mFAIL\033[0m  %s\n' "$*"; fail=$((fail + 1)); }
      warn() { printf '  \033[33mwarn\033[0m  %s\n' "$*"; warns=$((warns + 1)); }
      step() { printf '\n\033[1m%s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }
    If you call warn() you MUST define it -- a previous script called it without defining it and
    bash reported "warn: command not found" at 02:20.
  - A `--check` mode that performs assertions ONLY and changes nothing, exiting 0/1 with a VERDICT
    line. --check must be a real rehearsal: if the real run writes to a directory, --check must
    probe that it CAN write (create and remove a temp file), not merely test that the path exists.
    A rehearsal that skips the step that fails is not a rehearsal.
  - A final VERDICT line, green on success, red with a failure count otherwise.

COMMENTS: explain WHY, naming the specific failure the line prevents. Not "check the file exists"
but "the previous version asserted only that the pathname existed, which passed while systemd
refused to exec it and reported 203/EXEC, reading as a missing file".

HARD RULES, each learned from a real outage on this box:
  - LF line endings ONLY. No CRLF. No control bytes (nothing below 0x09 or between 0x0e and 0x1f).
    A stray CR produced `syntax error near unexpected token do\r`.
  - Never use `[ "$x" != prefix_* ]` to pattern-match. `[` compares STRINGS, so `*` is literal and
    the test is true for every value. Use `case`.
  - `cmd | grep -q` under `set -o pipefail`: grep exits at its first match, the pipe closes, and
    the upstream process dies of SIGPIPE (141). Do not require the upstream status to be 0.
  - `cmd >file 2>/dev/null` does NOT suppress a failed redirection -- bash reports that before the
    command runs. Group it: `{ cmd >file; } 2>/dev/null`.
  - A `while read` loop on the right of a pipe runs in a subshell and loses variable updates. Use
    `done < <(...)` or a heredoc.
  - Never build JSON by string concatenation. Use python3 -c with json.dumps.
  - Quote every variable expansion.


TESTS: vitest, files in tests/ named *.test.ts, run with `npx vitest run tests/<name>.test.ts`.
  - Assert PROPERTIES, not source text. A test that pins an exact variable name or an exact
    phrase fails against a correct rewrite and passes against a broken one. This has happened
    four times in this repo.
  - Strip whole-line comments before asserting on script text. A previous assertion passed
    against `# trap cleanup EXIT` because the raw text still contained the words. A check a
    comment can satisfy is not a check.
  - Where bash is available, RUN the script with spawnSync from node:child_process and assert on
    its exit status and output. spawnSync, not execFileSync: execFileSync returns only stdout and
    these scripts log to stderr. Guard with `it.runIf(BASH)` where BASH is detected once.
  - Shim external commands by writing a fake executable into a temp dir and prepending it to PATH.
    This is how the existing tests drive curl, systemctl and journalctl.
  - Include at least one CONTROL test that proves the check can fail: feed it the defect and
    require a failure. A check that never fails is not a check.
  - Do not weaken or delete an existing test to make yours pass. If an existing test blocks you,
    say so in your summary and stop.

Write the systemd unit pair that runs the off-host backup copy.

CREATE EXACTLY THESE 2 FILES with the write tool now; do not summarise or ask:
  1. deploy/fedbench-offhost.service
  2. deploy/fedbench-offhost.timer

The service runs `/usr/local/bin/backup-offhost.sh` (another task is writing that script; assume
it exists and takes `--dest`). The destination path is NOT known at authoring time, so the service
must read it from an environment file: `EnvironmentFile=-/etc/fedbench/offhost.env` defining
`FEDBENCH_OFFHOST_DEST`, and ExecStart passes `--dest ${FEDBENCH_OFFHOST_DEST}`. The leading `-`
makes the file optional so the unit still loads when it is absent.

Schedule it at 03:10 -- after the nightly dump at 02:20 (which has up to 15 minutes of randomised
delay) and before the Sunday restore drill at 03:40, so it copies a dump that is already complete
rather than racing the job writing it. Explain that reasoning in a comment.

It runs as `postgres`, the same user that owns the dumps (fedbench-backup.service runs as
postgres). It needs to READ /srv/fedbench/backups and WRITE the destination, which is not known
here -- so do not try to enumerate ReadWritePaths for the destination; instead explain in a
comment why ProtectSystem cannot be `strict` for this unit.

The destination is very likely a network filesystem, so a hung NFS mount must not wedge the unit
forever: set a TimeoutStartSec appropriate to copying a multi-GB file over a LAN, and say in a
comment why an unbounded timeout is the wrong choice for a network destination.


SYSTEMD RULES on this host (RHEL 9, SELinux enforcing), each learned from a real failure:
  - A `Type=oneshot` service driven by a timer must have NO [Install] section. The TIMER carries
    `[Install] WantedBy=timers.target`. Enabling a completed oneshot runs it at every boot.
  - `ExecStart=` must point into /usr/local/bin, never into a repo checkout or a service account's
    home. SELinux labels those `user_home_t` and systemd refuses to exec them, reporting
    `203/EXEC`, which reads as a missing file. /usr/local/bin is `bin_t`.
  - Every unit that can fail must carry `OnFailure=fedbench-alert@%n.service` in its [Unit]
    section. Without it a failure lands in a journal nobody reads. The backup failed three
    consecutive nights this way.
  - Install unit files with `cp`/`install`, NEVER `mv`: a moved file keeps its source SELinux
    context and systemd refuses to load it.
  - Timers get `Persistent=true` so an outage runs the missed job at next boot, and a
    `RandomizedDelaySec=` so simultaneous timers do not contend on the same disk.
  - Existing timer schedule, do not collide: fedbench-backup 02:20, fedbench-restore-drill Sun
    03:40, tailscale-cert 04:40, fedbench-deadman 09:15.
  - tests/deployUnitSafety.test.ts runs automatically over every *.service and *.timer in deploy/
    and will FAIL your unit if it breaks any of the above. Read that test file before writing.

CREATE EXACTLY THIS 1 FILE with the write tool now; do not summarise or ask:

  - Run `/usr/local/bin/backup-offhost.sh --check --dest <dest>` as the service user (postgres) via

  - The source tree is /srv/agni-data-vault/deploy (a real git checkout). Default
    `UNITSRC=${UNITSRC:-/srv/agni-data-vault/deploy}`.

Write an endpoint liveness probe and its tests.

CREATE EXACTLY THESE 2 FILES with the write tool now; do not summarise or ask:
  1. deploy/fedbench-healthz.sh
  2. tests/healthzProbe.test.ts

CONTEXT. The vault API on this host serves `/healthz` on 127.0.0.1:8099 and answers:
    {"ok":true,"checks":{"database":{"ok":true,"field_definitions":32}}}
On 2026-08-28 the box dropped off the network for five hours and nothing said a word. The daily
liveness check (deploy/fedbench-deadman.sh -- read it, and match its structure) watches backups and
timers but NOT whether the endpoint is actually serving.

WHAT fedbench-healthz.sh MUST DO:
  - Probe `${FEDBENCH_HEALTHZ_URL:-http://127.0.0.1:8099/healthz}` with curl, short timeout
    (default 10s, overridable).
  - Parse the response with python3 and json.load -- NOT grep. A body that is not JSON at all, or
    JSON with `ok:false`, or JSON missing the database check, must each be distinguished and
    reported differently. An HTTP 200 whose body says `ok:false` is a FAILURE: this codebase has
    already been bitten by exactly that shape, where Slack answers HTTP 200 with `{"ok":false}`
    in the body and `curl --fail` reported success.
  - Require the database check to be present and true, and require its row count to be greater
    than zero. A response reporting zero rows is the RLS-misconfiguration failure mode this system
    is designed around: every table has RLS enabled with no policies, so a role that loses
    BYPASSRLS reads NOTHING and every query returns empty with no error. Green-with-no-rows must
    be red.

  - FLAP SUPPRESSION, and this is the part that decides whether anyone keeps the alert switched
    on. The probe runs every few minutes. It must:
      * keep state under ${FEDBENCH_STATE_DIR:-/var/lib/fedbench};
      * only FAIL (exit non-zero) after N consecutive failures, default 3, so one dropped packet
        is not an alert;
      * NOT fail again on every subsequent run while the endpoint is still down -- alert on the
        transition into failure, not on the state. Re-alert only after a long interval (default 6
        hours) so a multi-day outage does not post every few minutes and get muted;
      * report RECOVERY: the first successful probe after a failing streak must say so on stdout
        (exit 0 -- recovery is not a failure), and reset the state.
    Document each of these choices in a comment saying what noise it prevents.
  - `--check` mode: probe once, report, and exit without touching state.
  - `--status` mode: print the current streak and last transition without probing.

WHAT tests/healthzProbe.test.ts MUST DO. Shim `curl` on PATH to return controlled bodies and
statuses, point FEDBENCH_STATE_DIR at a temp directory, and assert:
  - a healthy body exits 0;
  - `{"ok":false,...}` fails, as does a non-JSON body, as does a body whose database rowcount is 0;
  - the consecutive-failure threshold: two failures do NOT exit non-zero, the third does (this is
    the control that proves the threshold is real and not decorative);
  - after the alerting run, a further failing run does NOT exit non-zero again within the re-alert
    interval;
  - a success after failures reports recovery, exits 0, and resets the streak.

HARD RULES, each learned from a real outage on this box:
  - LF line endings ONLY. No CRLF. No control bytes (nothing below 0x09 or between 0x0e and 0x1f).
    A stray CR produced `syntax error near unexpected token do\r`.
  - Never use `[ "$x" != prefix_* ]` to pattern-match. `[` compares STRINGS, so `*` is literal and
    the test is true for every value. Use `case`.
  - `cmd | grep -q` under `set -o pipefail`: grep exits at its first match, the pipe closes, and
    the upstream process dies of SIGPIPE (141). Do not require the upstream status to be 0.
  - `cmd >file 2>/dev/null` does NOT suppress a failed redirection -- bash reports that before the
    command runs. Group it: `{ cmd >file; } 2>/dev/null`.
  - A `while read` loop on the right of a pipe runs in a subshell and loses variable updates. Use
    `done < <(...)` or a heredoc.
  - Never build JSON by string concatenation. Use python3 -c with json.dumps.
  - Quote every variable expansion.
